blocks.html: Part 1: Proving who is calling · Module 5
JWT validation
Last reviewed 2026-10-02 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can explain why a valid signature is not a valid token, write the profile a verifier must enforce before it sees any token, carry out the two classic algorithm attacks yourself, and test a verifier against the rejections it must make.

Before you start. You should know what an access token is and what it does not prove, from module 4. Module 2 covers HMAC and the difference between a shared secret and an asymmetric signature, which this module depends on.
Published lesson 6 of 33Complete the lesson and quick check, then record your progress.
Learn
1. The attack

Running example: ExampleHotels issues JWT access tokens, and its balance API verifies them. Company names are fictional.

A JWT carries its own description of itself. The header says which algorithm signed it. The payload says who issued it, who it is for, and when it expires. A verifier that reads those fields and believes them is doing what the token asked, not what the application needed. RFC 7519 makes this explicit: for every registered claim, including iss, aud and exp, it says "Use of this claim is OPTIONAL." A plain JWT is not required to contain anything.

So the verifier's behaviour depends on how much it decided in advance:

An attacker presentsVerifier trusts the headerAlgorithm allowlist onlyFull profile
A token with alg set to none and no signatureWorksBlockedBlocked
A token signed HS256, using the issuer's public key as the secretWorksBlockedBlocked
A genuine token issued for a different APIWorksWorksBlocked
A genuine token that expired an hour agoWorksWorksBlocked
An ID token where an access token was expectedWorksWorksBlocked
A current, genuine token stolen from the real clientWorksWorksWorks
The last row never turns green. Everything on this page checks that the token is genuine, not that the caller is its owner. Binding a token to its holder is module 7.
2. Why it works

Both algorithm attacks come from one mistake: letting the token choose the operation.

  • alg: none. RFC 7518 section 3.6 defines an Unsecured JWS, which uses the empty octet sequence as its signature. The specification is blunt about it: "Implementations MUST NOT accept Unsecured JWSs by default." A verifier that switches on the header's algorithm and has no branch for none other than "skip verification" accepts a token anyone can write.
  • RS256 to HS256 downgrade. This is algorithm confusion. The issuer signs with an RSA private key, and the verifier holds the matching public key. The public key is public. An attacker changes the header to HS256 and computes an HMAC over the token using that public key as the shared secret. A verifier that reads HS256 from the header and reaches for "the key it has" verifies successfully, because the attacker used the same value.

The remaining failures come from a different mistake: treating signature verification as the whole job.

  • "A valid signature means a valid token." It means the bytes were not altered since the issuer signed them. It says nothing about whether this token was meant for you, whether it is still current, or whether it is even the right kind of token.
  • "Every JWT has the claims I need." RFC 7519 marks all of them optional. Whether aud must be present is a decision your application makes, and if it does not make it, the answer is no.
  • "There is only one kind of token here." The same issuer commonly signs access tokens and ID tokens with the same key. Where one issuer can issue more than one kind of JWT, RFC 8725 section 3.12 requires the validation rules to be "mutually exclusive, rejecting JWTs of the wrong kind."
3. The control
What the application declares
Write the token profile down before any token arrives. Nothing in this list is ever read from the token being verified.

algorithms      RS256                      one entry, not a family
type            at+jwt                     RFC 9068 access token
issuer          https://auth.hotel.example exact match
audience        https://api.hotel.example  this API, not the family
required claims iss exp aud sub client_id iat jti
key source      the issuer's published keys, selected by kid
clock leeway    60 seconds, both directions
RFC 9068 section 2.2 is where the required claim list comes from. A different profile, such as an OpenID Connect ID token, has a different list and different rules.
How the verifier checks

1. Read the header's alg and compare it against the declared allowlist. Not on the list, including none: reject. Do not use it to select the operation; use it only to decide whether to continue.
  2. Check the typ against the declared type. This is what stops an ID token being accepted as an access token.
  3. Verify the signature with the declared algorithm and a key from the declared source, selected by kid. Getting the key from the token itself, through jku or x5u, hands the attacker the key choice.
  4. Only now read the claims. Confirm every required claim is present before testing any of them. A missing claim is a rejection, not a default.
  5. Compare iss with the expected issuer, and confirm the verifying key belongs to that issuer. RFC 8725 section 3.8 requires this pairing.
  6. Confirm this API's own identifier appears in aud. RFC 7519 section 4.1.3: if the claim is present and the principal is not identified by a value in it, "the JWT MUST be rejected."
  7. Check exp, and nbf and iat where present, against server time with a small, documented leeway.
  8. Hand the request to authorization. The token being genuine, current and addressed to you says nothing about whether this caller may perform this operation on this object.
The whole system
Untrusted inputServer decisionsDeclared stateRejection path
Two things arrive at the verifier, and only one of them is trusted. Everything the token says is a claim to be checked against the profile, never a setting to be obeyed.
4. Defaults and when to change them

DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
Allowed algorithmsA list with one entry, matching what your issuer actually signs withA key rotation introduces a second algorithm. Add it for the overlap, then remove the old one. Never widen to a family.
noneRejected, with no configuration that can turn it onNever. RFC 7518 section 3.6 says implementations must not accept Unsecured JWSs by default, and applications must not signal acceptance globally.
Token typetyp is at+jwt for OAuth access tokensYour issuer does not set it. Then say so in the profile and use another claim to distinguish token kinds, because something must.
Required claimsThe RFC 9068 list: iss exp aud sub client_id iat jtiYou are verifying a different kind of JWT. Write that profile separately; do not merge the two.
Key sourceThe issuer's published key set, fetched by the verifier, selected by kidNever take the key location from the token. jku and x5u in an untrusted header are attacker-controlled fetch targets.
Clock leeway60 seconds either directionTighten when clocks are synchronized and tokens are short lived. Widening past a few minutes means you are papering over a clock problem.
Error detail401 with no explanation of which check failedNever for callers. Log the specific reason internally with a correlation ID.
5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves: the token was signed by a key you expected, has not been altered since, is the kind of token you were expecting, was issued for you by an issuer you trust, and is current.

Doesn't prove: that the caller presenting it is the party it was issued to. It is still a bearer credential. It also does not prove the token has not been revoked since issuance, and it says nothing about whether this caller may touch this particular object.

Validation is not revocation. A verifier checking exp accepts a token until it expires, even if the account was disabled a minute after it was issued. Nothing on this page detects that. Deciding how fast a withdrawn grant must stop working, and what that costs, is module 6.
6. Prove it

A working verifier must reject every one of these. If any is accepted, the control is broken:

  • A token with alg set to none and an empty signature.
  • A token with alg changed to HS256 and signed with the issuer's public key as the secret.
  • A token with a valid signature but the wrong iss.
  • A token whose aud names another service, including one in the same family of APIs.
  • A token missing any claim the profile requires.
  • An ID token, or any other JWT kind the same issuer signs, presented where an access token is expected.
  • A token with one bit changed anywhere in the signature.
  • A token signed by a valid key belonging to a different issuer.
  • A token whose exp has passed, and one whose nbf has not yet arrived, both outside the declared leeway.
  • A token whose kid is unknown, or names a key that was rotated out.

Download labs/jwt_lab.py. Like module 3, this lab needs one package, because Python has no asymmetric cryptography in its standard library:

Install it into a virtual environment, so it does not change the Python the rest of your machine uses:

Windows              macOS and Linux
py -3 -m venv .venv          python3 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1    source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install cryptography==50.0.1
python labs/jwt_lab.py

Inside an activated environment use python, not py -3. The py command uses an active environment only when you have not asked for a version: "If you are running in an active virtual environment, have not requested a particular version, and there is no shebang line, the default runtime will be that virtual environment" (Python 3.14 documentation, Using Python on Windows, Python install manager, Basic use). Outside an environment, py -3 is still the right command on Windows.

Every module except 3, 5, 6 and 7 still needs nothing beyond Python 3. The lab generates an RSA key for the run, builds real tokens, and sends the same tokens past two verifiers. Keys, tokens and signatures stay in memory and are never printed.

$ python3 labs/jwt_lab.py
key source: RSA generated for this run; keys and tokens never printed

Part A: a verifier that reads the algorithm out of the token.
 1. genuine RS256 access token                 accept
 2. alg none, signature removed                accept
 3. alg HS256 signed with the public key       accept
 4. token issued for another audience          accept
 5. token that expired an hour ago             accept

Part B: a verifier that enforces a declared profile.
 6. genuine RS256 access token                 accept
 7. alg none, signature removed                reject: algorithm not allowed
 8. alg HS256 signed with the public key       reject: algorithm not allowed
 9. token issued for another audience          reject: audience mismatch
10. token that expired an hour ago             reject: expired
11. token from a different issuer              reject: issuer mismatch
12. an ID token where an access token is due   reject: wrong token type
13. required claim jti removed                 reject: missing claim jti
14. one bit flipped in the signature           reject: signature check failed
15. signed by a different RSA key              reject: signature check failed
16. nbf five minutes in the future             reject: not yet valid
17. expired 30s ago, inside 60s leeway         accept

all lab checks passed

Checks 2 and 3 are the two algorithm attacks, and part A is not a strawman: TrustingVerifier holds exactly one key and picks the operation from the token's header, which is how the defect appears in real code. Check 17 is the leeway working as intended, and is worth understanding before you tighten it. The lab runs every test in section 6 except the last. Its verifier holds one key and never reads kid, so it would accept an unknown one. Key selection is module 6's lab.

Try next:

  • Add "HS256" to ProfileVerifier.allowed_algorithms. The run exits 1 with one failure: check 8 still rejects, but the reason changes from reject: algorithm not allowed to reject: signature check failed. The confusion attack is not back, because this verifier always runs the RS256 check, whatever the header says. By widening one tuple you have removed one of the two controls that stopped it.
  • Delete the typ check. The run exits 1 with one failure: one check still rejects, for a different reason. Which token is now refused only because it happens to lack a claim, and what was it issued to do?
  • In ProfileVerifier.verify, move the claims = claims_of(token) line and the for name in self.required_claims loop under it, four lines in all, above the if not rs256_ok check. Everything still passes: exit 0, and all 17 checks print as before. Explain why that ordering is still wrong, using module 2's reasoning about the nonce cache.
8. Check your understanding

Why does signing with the public key work against a verifier that trusts the header?

The verifier holds one key and chooses the operation from the header. Told HS256, it treats its key as a shared secret and computes an HMAC. The attacker did the same thing with the same value, because a public key is public. The fix is not a better key, it is refusing to let the token pick the algorithm.

Your verifier checks the signature, issuer and expiry, and the token passes. Name two attacks still open.

A token issued for a different service in the same estate is accepted, because aud was not checked. And an ID token signed by the same issuer is accepted where an access token was expected, because the token type was not checked.

Why is a required-claim list part of the profile rather than a property of JWT?

Because RFC 7519 marks every registered claim OPTIONAL. A bare JWT can legitimately contain nothing. What must be present is decided by the profile you are verifying against, such as RFC 9068 for OAuth access tokens, and if you never declared one, you are not requiring anything.

The account is disabled one minute after a one-hour token is issued. What does your verifier do?

It keeps accepting the token for the remaining 59 minutes, plus the 60 seconds of leeway. Every check on this page passes, because they all describe the token, not the current state of the grant. Closing that window is revocation, in module 6.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. The verifier must decide the algorithm from its own configuration. Reading it from the token is what makes both alg none and the HS256 downgrade work.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. A longer key and a fresh key are both good practice, but neither helps when the verifier lets the token choose which operation to perform.

blocks.html:
Quick check

Stop the algorithm downgrade

An attacker changes a token's header to HS256 and signs it with the issuer's public key. Which change stops this?

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/jwt_lab.py and asks what the run prints. One of them changes nothing at all, and in two others the run fails but every token is still refused, for a different reason. In exercises 1 and 3 the cause is the same: the lab has no token that one version accepts and the other refuses, so the answer gives the measurement from a token that does.

1. The audience is checked with a substring test

In ProfileVerifier.verify, drop the list normalisation and test the audience against the claim directly:

if self.audience not in claims["aud"]:
    return "reject: audience mismatch"
What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Check 9 still rejects. Its audience is a different identifier that does not contain this service's own, so a substring test refuses it too.
  • Every aud in this lab is a string, so nothing raises, and a list would not raise either: in on a list is an exact match. The deleted line was there for the string case. It wraps a string in a list, so that in compares instead of searching.
  • Correct. Exit 0, 24 of 24 lines identical. Measured on a token this lab does not contain, with aud set to https://api.hotel.example.attacker.example: as published the verifier answers reject: audience mismatch, and with the substring test it answers accept. Anyone who can get a token issued for a name that starts with yours is then holding a token your service accepts. Check jwt-02 in the Reference layer says the audience is validated against this service's own identifier, which means compared, not searched.
  • Check 12 is refused on its typ header before any claim is read.

2. The leeway is subtracted from exp instead of added

In ProfileVerifier.verify, change the expiry test to now >= claims["exp"] - self.leeway.

Which check changes?

Every option, and why
  • Check 10 is an hour past expiry. It rejects under any sign of a 60 second leeway.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 17 goes from accept to reject: expired. Subtracting the leeway narrows the window instead of widening it, so the token is treated as expired 60 seconds before it actually is. This is the direction that fails safe, and it is still a bug: it is the one that produces intermittent rejections under clock skew, which is the hardest kind to diagnose in production. Check jwt-06 in the Reference layer asks for a documented leeway, and the direction is part of documenting it.
  • The nbf test has its own line, which this edit does not touch.
  • The edit moves the cutoff by 120 seconds, not 60, and check 17 sits inside that difference by design.

3. The typ header is not checked

In ProfileVerifier.verify, delete the two lines that reject a token whose typ is not at+jwt.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Not in this lab. The ID token it builds has no client_id, so the required-claim loop catches it a few lines later.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: the reason changes from reject: wrong token type to reject: missing claim client_id. The token is still refused, by accident, because this particular ID token happens to lack a claim the profile requires. Measured on a token the lab does not contain, with typ set to JWT but every access-token claim present: as published the verifier answers reject: wrong token type, and without the typ check it answers accept. Check jwt-05 in the Reference layer asks for mutually exclusive rules per token kind, and a claim that happens to be absent is not a rule.
  • They cover it for this one token. That is the difference between a control and a coincidence.
  • Check 13 removes jti from an otherwise correct access token, and its typ is already right.

4. The allowlist is taken from the token header

In ProfileVerifier.verify, compare the header's alg against a list built from that same header, so the allowlist can never refuse anything. Leave the RS256 signature check as it is.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • It is not, and the reason matters: this verifier always calls the RS256 check, whatever the header says. The attack in Part A works because that verifier picks its verification routine from the header too. Removing the allowlist alone is not enough to reproduce it.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures, both reasons only: checks 7 and 8 go from reject: algorithm not allowed to reject: signature check failed. The unsigned token has nothing for RS256 to verify, and the HS256 token's MAC is not an RSA signature. Two independent controls, the allowlist and a hardcoded verification routine, and either one alone stops these tokens. That is why check jwt-01 in the Reference layer is written about where the algorithm comes from rather than about which algorithms are refused.
  • Part A does accept them, and that is a different verifier. Part B is the one being edited.
  • Both change. Neither token's signature survives an RSA verification.
Course progress: return to the course dashboard to see your published-module progress.
Reference
Controls
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

• StandardThe caller must be able to specify a supported set of algorithms, and no others may be used. RFC 8725 section 3.1, which also requires that the alg header specifies the same algorithm actually used.
  • StandardApplications must only allow cryptographically current algorithms that meet their security requirements. RFC 8725 section 3.2.
  • StandardImplementations must not accept Unsecured JWSs, the alg value none, by default, and applications must not signal acceptance of them at a global level. RFC 7518 section 3.6.
  • StandardWhen a JWT contains iss, the application must validate that the keys used belong to that issuer, and must reject the JWT if they do not. RFC 8725 section 3.8.
  • StandardWhere one issuer can issue JWTs for more than one relying party, the audience value must be validated, and the JWT rejected if the audience is absent or not associated with the recipient. RFC 8725 section 3.9. RFC 7519 section 4.1.3 says that when aud is present, the JWT must be rejected if the principal is not identified by a value in it.
  • StandardWhere one issuer can issue more than one kind of JWT, the validation rules must be mutually exclusive and reject JWTs of the wrong kind. RFC 8725 section 3.12. Explicit typing is covered in section 3.11.
  • StandardThe current time must be before exp. RFC 7519 section 4.1.4, which allows a small leeway for clock skew.
  • StandardAn OAuth JWT access token requires iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat and jti, and RFC 9068 section 2.1 requires the typ header to carry the access token media type, recommending the short form at+jwt. Section 4 requires the resource server to reject a token whose typ is neither at+jwt nor application/at+jwt. Under RFC 9068 section 2.2, a client credentials token still has sub, and the RFC recommends that it identify the client rather than a user.
  • BaselineDeclare the whole profile in configuration: algorithms, type, issuer, audience, required claims, key source and leeway. Read none of it from the token.
  • BaselineVerify in this order: algorithm allowlist, token type, signature, required claims present, then claim values. Reject before reading anything you have not yet authenticated.
  • BaselineSelect the key from the issuer's published key set by kid. Never follow jku or x5u from the token header.
  • BaselineAllow 60 seconds of clock leeway in both directions, and document it.
  • BaselineReturn 401 with no indication of which check failed. Log the specific reason with a correlation ID.
  • OptionUse a reviewed JWT library rather than writing the parsing yourself, and configure its algorithm, audience and issuer options explicitly, because most default to checking less than this list.
  • OptionSender-constrain the token with mTLS or DPoP where theft is a material risk. Module 7.
Review checklist items
These are collected into the site checklist.

• The verifier selects the algorithm from its own allowlist, never from the token header Test a token with alg set to none and one downgraded to HS256 and signed with the issuer's public key. Both must be rejected.
  • The audience is validated against this service's own identifier A genuine token issued for a sibling service in the same estate is rejected. A missing aud is rejected.
  • The signing key comes from the issuer's published key set, selected by kid The verifier never fetches a key named by jku or x5u in the token header. An unknown kid is rejected.
  • The token profile is declared, and every required claim is checked for presence before use Name the profile, such as RFC 9068 for OAuth access tokens. A token missing any required claim is rejected rather than defaulted.
  • Different kinds of JWT from the same issuer have mutually exclusive validation rules An ID token is rejected where an access token is expected, and the reverse. Token type or an equivalent claim is checked.
  • Issuer and time claims are validated with a documented leeway iss matches exactly, the key belongs to that issuer, and exp, nbf and iat are checked against server time.
  • Rejection responses do not say which check failed Callers get 401. The specific reason is logged internally with a correlation ID.
  • Library defaults have been read, not assumed Confirm what your JWT library validates by default, and configure algorithms, audience and issuer explicitly. Test the negative cases against your own configuration.
Sources

• RFC 7519: JSON Web Token (JWT), May 2015. Updated by RFC 7797 and RFC 8725. Sections 4.1.1 to 4.1.7, where every registered claim is OPTIONAL, and 4.1.3 and 4.1.4.
  • RFC 7518: JSON Web Algorithms (JWA), May 2015. Updated by RFC 9864 (October 2025), which deprecates the EdDSA identifier and adds a review rule for the algorithm registry. It does not change section 3.6 or RS256. Section 3.6, the none algorithm and Unsecured JWSs.
  • RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices, Best Current Practice, February 2020. Sections 3.1, 3.2, 3.8, 3.9, 3.11, 3.12.
  • RFC 9068: JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens, October 2021. Sections 2.1, 2.2, 4.
  • pyca/cryptography 50.0.1 documentation: RSA. Used for key generation, signing and verification in the lab.
  • Python 3.14 documentation: Using Python on Windows. Python install manager, Basic use: how the py command picks a runtime when a virtual environment is active.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Proves: the token was signed by a key you expected, has not been altered since, is the kind of token you were expecting, was issued for you by an issuer you trust, and is current.

Doesn't prove: that the caller presenting it is the party it was issued to. It is still a bearer credential. It also does not prove the token has not been revoked since issuance, and it says nothing about whether this caller may touch this particular object.

Validation is not revocation. A verifier checking exp accepts a token until it expires, even if the account was disabled a minute after it was issued. Nothing on this page detects that. Deciding how fast a withdrawn grant must stop working, and what that costs, is module 6.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
A working verifier must reject every one of these. If any is accepted, the control is broken:

  • A token with alg set to none and an empty signature.
  • A token with alg changed to HS256 and signed with the issuer's public key as the secret.
  • A token with a valid signature but the wrong iss.
  • A token whose aud names another service, including one in the same family of APIs.
  • A token missing any claim the profile requires.
  • An ID token, or any other JWT kind the same issuer signs, presented where an access token is expected.
  • A token with one bit changed anywhere in the signature.
  • A token signed by a valid key belonging to a different issuer.
  • A token whose exp has passed, and one whose nbf has not yet arrived, both outside the declared leeway.
  • A token whose kid is unknown, or names a key that was rotated out.

sections.heading: 7. Lab
sections.html:
Download labs/jwt_lab.py. Like module 3, this lab needs one package, because Python has no asymmetric cryptography in its standard library:

Install it into a virtual environment, so it does not change the Python the rest of your machine uses:

Windows              macOS and Linux
py -3 -m venv .venv          python3 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1    source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install cryptography==50.0.1
python labs/jwt_lab.py

Inside an activated environment use python, not py -3. The py command uses an active environment only when you have not asked for a version: "If you are running in an active virtual environment, have not requested a particular version, and there is no shebang line, the default runtime will be that virtual environment" (Python 3.14 documentation, Using Python on Windows, Python install manager, Basic use). Outside an environment, py -3 is still the right command on Windows.

Every module except 3, 5, 6 and 7 still needs nothing beyond Python 3. The lab generates an RSA key for the run, builds real tokens, and sends the same tokens past two verifiers. Keys, tokens and signatures stay in memory and are never printed.

$ python3 labs/jwt_lab.py
key source: RSA generated for this run; keys and tokens never printed

Part A: a verifier that reads the algorithm out of the token.
 1. genuine RS256 access token                 accept
 2. alg none, signature removed                accept
 3. alg HS256 signed with the public key       accept
 4. token issued for another audience          accept
 5. token that expired an hour ago             accept

Part B: a verifier that enforces a declared profile.
 6. genuine RS256 access token                 accept
 7. alg none, signature removed                reject: algorithm not allowed
 8. alg HS256 signed with the public key       reject: algorithm not allowed
 9. token issued for another audience          reject: audience mismatch
10. token that expired an hour ago             reject: expired
11. token from a different issuer              reject: issuer mismatch
12. an ID token where an access token is due   reject: wrong token type
13. required claim jti removed                 reject: missing claim jti
14. one bit flipped in the signature           reject: signature check failed
15. signed by a different RSA key              reject: signature check failed
16. nbf five minutes in the future             reject: not yet valid
17. expired 30s ago, inside 60s leeway         accept

all lab checks passed

Checks 2 and 3 are the two algorithm attacks, and part A is not a strawman: TrustingVerifier holds exactly one key and picks the operation from the token's header, which is how the defect appears in real code. Check 17 is the leeway working as intended, and is worth understanding before you tighten it. The lab runs every test in section 6 except the last. Its verifier holds one key and never reads kid, so it would accept an unknown one. Key selection is module 6's lab.

Try next:

  • Add "HS256" to ProfileVerifier.allowed_algorithms. The run exits 1 with one failure: check 8 still rejects, but the reason changes from reject: algorithm not allowed to reject: signature check failed. The confusion attack is not back, because this verifier always runs the RS256 check, whatever the header says. By widening one tuple you have removed one of the two controls that stopped it.
  • Delete the typ check. The run exits 1 with one failure: one check still rejects, for a different reason. Which token is now refused only because it happens to lack a claim, and what was it issued to do?
  • In ProfileVerifier.verify, move the claims = claims_of(token) line and the for name in self.required_claims loop under it, four lines in all, above the if not rs256_ok check. Everything still passes: exit 0, and all 17 checks print as before. Explain why that ordering is still wrong, using module 2's reasoning about the nonce cache.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
Why does signing with the public key work against a verifier that trusts the header?

The verifier holds one key and chooses the operation from the header. Told HS256, it treats its key as a shared secret and computes an HMAC. The attacker did the same thing with the same value, because a public key is public. The fix is not a better key, it is refusing to let the token pick the algorithm.

Your verifier checks the signature, issuer and expiry, and the token passes. Name two attacks still open.

A token issued for a different service in the same estate is accepted, because aud was not checked. And an ID token signed by the same issuer is accepted where an access token was expected, because the token type was not checked.

Why is a required-claim list part of the profile rather than a property of JWT?

Because RFC 7519 marks every registered claim OPTIONAL. A bare JWT can legitimately contain nothing. What must be present is decided by the profile you are verifying against, such as RFC 9068 for OAuth access tokens, and if you never declared one, you are not requiring anything.

The account is disabled one minute after a one-hour token is issued. What does your verifier do?

It keeps accepting the token for the remaining 59 minutes, plus the 60 seconds of leeway. Every check on this page passes, because they all describe the token, not the current state of the grant. Closing that window is revocation, in module 6.

Quick check

sections.heading: Stop the algorithm downgrade
sections.html:
An attacker changes a token's header to HS256 and signs it with the issuer's public key. Which change stops this?

Exercises

sections.heading: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.heading_text: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.html:
Each exercise edits one place in labs/jwt_lab.py and asks what the run prints. One of them changes nothing at all, and in two others the run fails but every token is still refused, for a different reason. In exercises 1 and 3 the cause is the same: the lab has no token that one version accepts and the other refuses, so the answer gives the measurement from a token that does.

1. The audience is checked with a substring test

In ProfileVerifier.verify, drop the list normalisation and test the audience against the claim directly:

if self.audience not in claims["aud"]:
    return "reject: audience mismatch"
What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Check 9 still rejects. Its audience is a different identifier that does not contain this service's own, so a substring test refuses it too.
  • Every aud in this lab is a string, so nothing raises, and a list would not raise either: in on a list is an exact match. The deleted line was there for the string case. It wraps a string in a list, so that in compares instead of searching.
  • Correct. Exit 0, 24 of 24 lines identical. Measured on a token this lab does not contain, with aud set to https://api.hotel.example.attacker.example: as published the verifier answers reject: audience mismatch, and with the substring test it answers accept. Anyone who can get a token issued for a name that starts with yours is then holding a token your service accepts. Check jwt-02 in the Reference layer says the audience is validated against this service's own identifier, which means compared, not searched.
  • Check 12 is refused on its typ header before any claim is read.

2. The leeway is subtracted from exp instead of added

In ProfileVerifier.verify, change the expiry test to now >= claims["exp"] - self.leeway.

Which check changes?

Every option, and why
  • Check 10 is an hour past expiry. It rejects under any sign of a 60 second leeway.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 17 goes from accept to reject: expired. Subtracting the leeway narrows the window instead of widening it, so the token is treated as expired 60 seconds before it actually is. This is the direction that fails safe, and it is still a bug: it is the one that produces intermittent rejections under clock skew, which is the hardest kind to diagnose in production. Check jwt-06 in the Reference layer asks for a documented leeway, and the direction is part of documenting it.
  • The nbf test has its own line, which this edit does not touch.
  • The edit moves the cutoff by 120 seconds, not 60, and check 17 sits inside that difference by design.

3. The typ header is not checked

In ProfileVerifier.verify, delete the two lines that reject a token whose typ is not at+jwt.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Not in this lab. The ID token it builds has no client_id, so the required-claim loop catches it a few lines later.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: the reason changes from reject: wrong token type to reject: missing claim client_id. The token is still refused, by accident, because this particular ID token happens to lack a claim the profile requires. Measured on a token the lab does not contain, with typ set to JWT but every access-token claim present: as published the verifier answers reject: wrong token type, and without the typ check it answers accept. Check jwt-05 in the Reference layer asks for mutually exclusive rules per token kind, and a claim that happens to be absent is not a rule.
  • They cover it for this one token. That is the difference between a control and a coincidence.
  • Check 13 removes jti from an otherwise correct access token, and its typ is already right.

4. The allowlist is taken from the token header

In ProfileVerifier.verify, compare the header's alg against a list built from that same header, so the allowlist can never refuse anything. Leave the RS256 signature check as it is.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • It is not, and the reason matters: this verifier always calls the RS256 check, whatever the header says. The attack in Part A works because that verifier picks its verification routine from the header too. Removing the allowlist alone is not enough to reproduce it.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures, both reasons only: checks 7 and 8 go from reject: algorithm not allowed to reject: signature check failed. The unsigned token has nothing for RS256 to verify, and the HS256 token's MAC is not an RSA signature. Two independent controls, the allowlist and a hardcoded verification routine, and either one alone stops these tokens. That is why check jwt-01 in the Reference layer is written about where the algorithm comes from rather than about which algorithms are refused.
  • Part A does accept them, and that is a different verifier. Part B is the one being edited.
  • Both change. Neither token's signature survives an RSA verification.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • StandardThe caller must be able to specify a supported set of algorithms, and no others may be used. RFC 8725 section 3.1, which also requires that the alg header specifies the same algorithm actually used.
  • StandardApplications must only allow cryptographically current algorithms that meet their security requirements. RFC 8725 section 3.2.
  • StandardImplementations must not accept Unsecured JWSs, the alg value none, by default, and applications must not signal acceptance of them at a global level. RFC 7518 section 3.6.
  • StandardWhen a JWT contains iss, the application must validate that the keys used belong to that issuer, and must reject the JWT if they do not. RFC 8725 section 3.8.
  • StandardWhere one issuer can issue JWTs for more than one relying party, the audience value must be validated, and the JWT rejected if the audience is absent or not associated with the recipient. RFC 8725 section 3.9. RFC 7519 section 4.1.3 says that when aud is present, the JWT must be rejected if the principal is not identified by a value in it.
  • StandardWhere one issuer can issue more than one kind of JWT, the validation rules must be mutually exclusive and reject JWTs of the wrong kind. RFC 8725 section 3.12. Explicit typing is covered in section 3.11.
  • StandardThe current time must be before exp. RFC 7519 section 4.1.4, which allows a small leeway for clock skew.
  • StandardAn OAuth JWT access token requires iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat and jti, and RFC 9068 section 2.1 requires the typ header to carry the access token media type, recommending the short form at+jwt. Section 4 requires the resource server to reject a token whose typ is neither at+jwt nor application/at+jwt. Under RFC 9068 section 2.2, a client credentials token still has sub, and the RFC recommends that it identify the client rather than a user.
  • BaselineDeclare the whole profile in configuration: algorithms, type, issuer, audience, required claims, key source and leeway. Read none of it from the token.
  • BaselineVerify in this order: algorithm allowlist, token type, signature, required claims present, then claim values. Reject before reading anything you have not yet authenticated.
  • BaselineSelect the key from the issuer's published key set by kid. Never follow jku or x5u from the token header.
  • BaselineAllow 60 seconds of clock leeway in both directions, and document it.
  • BaselineReturn 401 with no indication of which check failed. Log the specific reason with a correlation ID.
  • OptionUse a reviewed JWT library rather than writing the parsing yourself, and configure its algorithm, audience and issuer options explicitly, because most default to checking less than this list.
  • OptionSender-constrain the token with mTLS or DPoP where theft is a material risk. Module 7.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • The verifier selects the algorithm from its own allowlist, never from the token header Test a token with alg set to none and one downgraded to HS256 and signed with the issuer's public key. Both must be rejected.
  • The audience is validated against this service's own identifier A genuine token issued for a sibling service in the same estate is rejected. A missing aud is rejected.
  • The signing key comes from the issuer's published key set, selected by kid The verifier never fetches a key named by jku or x5u in the token header. An unknown kid is rejected.
  • The token profile is declared, and every required claim is checked for presence before use Name the profile, such as RFC 9068 for OAuth access tokens. A token missing any required claim is rejected rather than defaulted.
  • Different kinds of JWT from the same issuer have mutually exclusive validation rules An ID token is rejected where an access token is expected, and the reverse. Token type or an equivalent claim is checked.
  • Issuer and time claims are validated with a documented leeway iss matches exactly, the key belongs to that issuer, and exp, nbf and iat are checked against server time.
  • Rejection responses do not say which check failed Callers get 401. The specific reason is logged internally with a correlation ID.
  • Library defaults have been read, not assumed Confirm what your JWT library validates by default, and configure algorithms, audience and issuer explicitly. Test the negative cases against your own configuration.

quiz.summary: Why does signing with the public key work against a verifier that trusts the header?
quiz.html:
Why does signing with the public key work against a verifier that trusts the header?

The verifier holds one key and chooses the operation from the header. Told HS256, it treats its key as a shared secret and computes an HMAC. The attacker did the same thing with the same value, because a public key is public. The fix is not a better key, it is refusing to let the token pick the algorithm.

quiz.summary: Your verifier checks the signature, issuer and expiry, and the token passes. Name two attacks still open.
quiz.html:
Your verifier checks the signature, issuer and expiry, and the token passes. Name two attacks still open.

A token issued for a different service in the same estate is accepted, because aud was not checked. And an ID token signed by the same issuer is accepted where an access token was expected, because the token type was not checked.

quiz.summary: Why is a required-claim list part of the profile rather than a property of JWT?
quiz.html:
Why is a required-claim list part of the profile rather than a property of JWT?

Because RFC 7519 marks every registered claim OPTIONAL. A bare JWT can legitimately contain nothing. What must be present is decided by the profile you are verifying against, such as RFC 9068 for OAuth access tokens, and if you never declared one, you are not requiring anything.
